subject: Svenska 2
title: Expository and argumentative text
sourceSummary: Structure for expository text, source handling in running text, the difference between examining and arguing, and paragraphing and coherence.

questions.prompt: What is the most important difference between an expository text and an argumentative text?
questions.opener: One wants to show several sides, the other wants to win you over.
choices: They are the same text type with different names
An expository text sheds light on a question objectively and from all sides, an argumentative text argues for a thesis and wants to persuade
An expository text must never contain facts
An argumentative text always lacks a clear structure
questions.explanation: An expository text sheds light on a question objectively and from all sides without necessarily taking a position, while an argumentative text has a clear thesis that the author wants to persuade the reader of.

questions.prompt: Which structure does an expository text most often follow?
questions.opener: Consider how an examination should be followable by a reader who has not already made up their mind.
choices: Just one long, continuous argument without any division
Only a summary of other people's opinions without any structure of its own
Verse, chorus, verse
An introduction with the question at issue, an expository section shedding light on different perspectives, and a concluding conclusion
questions.explanation: An expository text often opens with a question or purpose, is followed by an expository section in which different perspectives and facts are weighed against each other, and ends with a conclusion or summarising reflection.

questions.prompt: What characterises good source handling in running text?
questions.opener: The source should support your reasoning, not take it over.
choices: Sources are woven naturally into the text and clearly indicated, rather than just stacked up as a list
You rewrite other people's texts without stating where the information comes from
You quote as much as possible word for word to avoid writing yourself
Sources only need to be stated in an appendix, never in the text
questions.explanation: Good source handling means sources are integrated naturally into the running text — through rewording, summary or short quotations — while it is clearly stated where the information comes from. Just stacking up quotations or omitting source references weakens credibility.

questions.prompt: A student rewrites a sentence from an article with almost exactly the same word choices, without quotation marks or a source reference. What is the problem?
questions.opener: Ask yourself whether a reader can tell what is yours and what is someone else's.
choices: No problem, it's enough to have read the article
The only problem is that the sentence is too short
It counts as plagiarism since the source is neither quoted correctly nor cited
It's only a problem if the article is written in another language
questions.explanation: Reproducing someone else's phrasing almost word for word without quotation marks and a source reference counts as plagiarism, regardless of how carefully you have read the source. Text should either be clearly reworded in your own words with a source reference, or quoted correctly.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of clear paragraphing in an expository text?
questions.opener: What happens to readability if everything is one single long block of text?
choices: To make the text longer
So that each paragraph conveys one main idea and creates a logical, readable structure
To avoid having to write a coherent conclusion
Paragraphing has no bearing on readability
questions.explanation: Clear paragraphing makes a text easier to follow — each paragraph should be built around one main idea, and the paragraphs should connect logically with the help of linking words and a common thread running through the text.

questions.prompt: An argumentative text actively addresses the strongest counterarguments before restating its thesis. What purpose does this serve?
questions.opener: What does it say about a writer who dares to raise counterarguments?
choices: It weakens the text's credibility since counterarguments should never be mentioned
It is just a way of making the text longer with no real purpose
Counterarguments should always be placed right at the very start of the text
It strengthens the text's credibility by showing that the author is aware of, and can address, objections
questions.explanation: Addressing counterarguments shows that the writer is well informed and has considered different perspectives, which strengthens the text's credibility and the force of the argument — rather than simply ignoring objections.

questions.prompt: A text is headed "Should schools ban mobile phones in the classroom?" and weighs advantages and disadvantages against each other without taking a clear position at the end. Another text with the same heading arrives at a clear position: schools should ban phones. Analyse which text type each text belongs to and why.
questions.opener: Look at whether the text arrives at a thesis or stops at a weighing-up.
questions.answer: The first text is expository because it sheds light on the pros and cons from all sides without taking a position. The second is argumentative because it has a clear thesis (a phone ban) that it tries to persuade the reader of.
steps: Expository text: the purpose is to shed light on a question objectively from several angles, often without a final position — the text stops at a weighing-up.
Argumentative text: the purpose is to persuade — the text has a clear thesis backed up with arguments directed towards a specific position.
The same topic (mobile phones in the classroom) can therefore be treated in both text types — it is the purpose and structure, not the topic, that determines the text type.
A common misconception is that an expository text has no opinions at all — it may well have a concluding reflection, but it still weighs in several perspectives rather than arguing for a thesis.

questions.prompt: Summarise the basics of good source handling and structure in expository and argumentative text.
questions.opener: Structure and sources — the two things that determine whether a text holds up.
questions.answer: Expository text: shedding light on a question from all sides, structure of introduction–examination–conclusion · Argumentative text: clear thesis, arguments, addressing counterarguments, a closing restatement of the thesis · Source handling: weave sources naturally into running text, always state where information comes from, avoid near-word-for-word rewording without quotation marks (plagiarism) · Paragraphing: each paragraph one main idea, linking words create a common thread running through the whole text.
